lines.text: And a ship sailing on a blue sea.
Another gust of rainy wind blew into the tree house.
“I wish we were there instead of here,” she said.
Sitting on a branch outside the window ledge of the tree house was a green parrot.
Exactly like the parrot in the picture.
Suddenly the wind started to whistle.
The tree house started to spin.
Jack felt hot sunlight streaming into the tree house.
He heard the sound of waves.
He and Annie looked out the window.
The tree house was in a palm tree.
Beyond was a bright blue sea.
A tall sailing ship was on the horizon.
It was just like the picture in the book.
Polly was flying in circles above the tree house.
Then she swooped down to the ocean.
She took off her raincoat and dropped it on the floor.
“Wait, we have to study the book first,” said Jack.
He started to reach for the book.
“You can read it on the beach,” she said.
Without even looking at the cover, she shoved the book into Jack’s backpack.
Actually, the water did look wonderful.
He took off his raincoat, too.
Annie handed Jack his backpack, then started down the ladder.
Jack folded the raincoat and put it next to the stack of books.
Then he went down the ladder.
As soon as Annie hit the sand, she ran toward the ocean.
Jack watched her wade into the water.
She was still wearing her rain boots.
Jack took off his boots and socks.
He put them beside his pack.
Then he rolled up his jeans.
And ran across the hot sand into the waves.
The water was warm and clear.
Jack could see shells and tiny fishes.
He shielded his eyes against the sun.
And peered out at the sea.
The tall sailing ship seemed a bit closer.
Not over the bright blue sea.
When Jack looked out at the sea again, the ship seemed even closer.
Now Jack could see its flag.
As he stared at the ship’s flag, a chill went through him.
He started out of the water.
He grabbed the book from his backpack.
For the first time, he and Annie read the title of the book.
“Pirates of the Caribbean,” Jack read aloud.
“We’ve come to the time of pirates!”
Jack flipped to the picture that showed the parrot, the sea and the ship.
He read the caption under the picture: Three hundred years ago, pirates raided Spanish treasure ships in the Caribbean Sea.
He grabbed his notebook and pencil from his pack.
He wrote: He turned to the next page.
There was a picture of a pirate flag.
He read: The skull-and-crossbones flag was called the Jolly Roger.
“I want to make a drawing of the flag.”
He propped the pirate book in the sand.
He started drawing the Jolly Roger flag.
“Don’t copy the picture in the book,” said Annie.
But Jack pushed his glasses into place and kept drawing.
“Jack, some pirates are getting into a rowboat,” said Annie.
“Jack, the boat’s leaving the big ship,” said Annie.
He saw the rowboat coming toward the shore.
She started running toward the tree house.
Jack went down on his knees.
Jack saw something glinting in the sand.
Then he threw his notebook and pencil into his pack.
He put the pack on his back.
He grabbed his boots and his socks.
Annie was at the top of the rope ladder.
Jack looked back at the sea.
The pirates were closer to the shore.
Suddenly Jack saw the pirate book.
In all the confusion he had forgotten it.
It was still propped in the sand.
He dropped his socks and boots below the tree house.
But Jack was already running toward the water.
Jack shoved the book into his backpack.
Suddenly a giant wave carried the rowboat right onto the beach.
Three big pirates splashed onto the sand.
They had knives in their teeth.
They had pistols in their belts.
Jack started to run across the hot sand.
He ran as fast as he could.
Before Jack knew it, the biggest pirate had grabbed him!
But the pirate had huge, strong arms.
He held on to Jack and laughed a mean, ugly laugh.
He had a shaggy black beard.
He saw her coming down the rope ladder.
The other two pirates laughed meanly.
Annie charged up to the biggest pirate.
She hit the pirate with her fist and kicked him.
And with his giant hands, he held Jack and Annie as if they were two kittens.
Then he turned to the other two.
“Find out what’s in their house, you dogs,” he said.
And they started up the ladder to the tree house.
“Dogs are nicer than you,” said Annie.
He spit on the sand again.
A gleeful shriek pierced the air.
Pinky leaned out the tree house window.
Cap’n Bones dropped Jack and Annie.
He caught the medallion as it fell.
Cap’n Bones threw back his head and laughed horribly.
He grabbed two of his pistols.
He shot them into the air.
Pinky and Stinky howled like wolves.
Jack and Annie watched in horror.
The gold-greedy pirates seemed to have lost their minds.
Together they started to back slowly away from the pirates.
He aimed his pistols at them.
Cap’n Bones grinned his black-toothed grin.
“Tell old Bones where the rest is,” he growled.
He reached into a belt pouch and pulled out a torn piece of paper.
He waved it at Jack and Annie.
“Aye, it’s the map telling about Kidd’s treasure.”
“We don’t know anything about a kid’s treasure.”
Cap’n Bones shoved the map in Jack’s face.
Jack stared at the strange marks on the paper.
Jack pointed at the words at the bottom of the map.
“Well, it means … ” Cap’n Bones’ good eye squinted at the writing.
“Aw, leave him alone,” Pinky growled at Jack.
“You know he can’t read,” said Stinky.
Cap’n Bones roared at his men.
“Jack and I can read,” Annie piped up.
Cap’n Bones gave Jack and Annie a dark look.
The pirate squinted his good eye.
When the treasure’s in me hands, I’ll let you go.”
“It says, The gold doth lie beneath the whale’s eye.”
“They can rot there till they’re ready to tell us how to find Kidd’s treasure!”
Jack and Annie were tossed into the rowboat.
The sky ahead was dark with thunderclouds.
A strong wind had started to blow.
Pinky and Stinky began rowing toward the big ship.
Polly the parrot was flying over the sand.
“She wants to help us,” whispered Annie.
Polly started to fly out over the waves.
But the winds were too strong.
She turned around and flew back to the island.
The rowboat tossed from side to side.
“Or we’ll be meat for those evil brutes!”
Dark fins cut through the water.
One zoomed right by the boat.
Jack could have reached out and touched it.
Soon the rowboat pulled alongside the ship.
The air was filled with wild fiddle music and bagpipes playing.
And Jack heard jeers, shouts, and ugly laughter.
Cap’n Bones shouted to his men.
Annie and Jack were hauled onto the deck.
It rolled from side to side.
Ropes flapped and snapped in the wild wind.
Everywhere they looked, Jack and Annie saw pirates.
A couple of pirates grabbed Jack and Annie.
And threw them in the ship’s cabin.
The air inside the cabin was damp and sour-smelling.
A shaft of gray light came through a small round window.
“We’ve got to figure out how to get back to the island.”
“So we can get into the tree house and go home,” said Annie.
How would they ever get out of this mess?
“We better examine the book,” he said.
He reached into his pack and pulled out the pirate book.
He looked for information to help them.
He found a picture of pirates burying a treasure chest.
Together they read the words under the picture.
Captain Kidd was a famous pirate.
It is said that he buried a treasure chest on a deserted island.
The chest was filled with gold and jewels.
“So that’s the kid that Bones keeps talking about,” said Annie.
Annie looked out the round window.
“And Captain Kidd’s treasure is buried somewhere on the island,” she said.
Jack took out his notebook and pencil.
He looked back at the book.
As big as a football field.”
Jack jumped up and looked out the window with her.
All he could see was the island.
The island is shaped like a giant whale!”
The slope of the island looked like the back of a whale.
The palm tree that held the tree house looked like the spout of the whale.
A big black rock looked like the eye of the whale.
“The gold doth lie beneath the whale’s eye,” whispered Jack.
“So the treasure must be under that rock,” said Annie.
“Now we just have to get back to the island.
We’ll show Cap’n Bones where the treasure is.
Then while all the pirates are digging, we’ll sneak up to the tree house.”
“And make a wish to go home,” said Annie.
Jack poked his head out of the round window of the cabin.
The pirates took up the cry.
Cap’n Bones stuck his ugly face through the window.
His good eye glared at Jack.
“We’re ready to tell the truth, sir,” said Jack.
“We know where Captain Kidd’s treasure is.”
We have to show you,” said Annie.
Cap’n Bones gave Annie and Jack a long hard look.
Then he roared at his men, “Get some rope and shovels!”
“Then throw these lubbers in the boat!
We’re going back to the island!”
Back in the rowboat, Jack saw the sky had grown even darker with clouds.
“You’ll see a gale if I don’t get me gold today, by thunder!”
The three pirates battled the waves, until the rowboat reached the island.
They all piled onto the shore.
Cap’n Bones grabbed Jack and Annie.
“Now show us where the treasure is.”
She pointed at the black rock near the tip of the island.
Cap’n Bones dragged Jack and Annie down the beach to the black rock.
Cap’n Bones said to Pinky and Stinky.
How could they get away from him?
“Don’t you think you should help your friends?”
Cap’n Bones gave Jack a horrible grin.
I’m going to hold you two—till there’s treasure in me hands!”
Pinky and Stinky tied their rope around the big rock.
“Aghh, let the dogs do the work!”
“You’re not very nice to them,” said Annie.
They started pulling the rock across the sand.
“Now let’s dig where the rock was,” said Jack.
But Cap’n Bones ignored his suggestion.
Pinky and Stinky started to dig.
There was going to be a thunderstorm.
I got sand in me eyes!”
He held Jack and Annie with one hand.
With the other he pulled out the gold medallion.
He tossed it at the two pirates.
“Dig for more of these, you swine!”
Stinky and Pinky looked up at the parrot.
“We’ve got to get to the ship before it’s too late!”
The two pirates threw down their shovels.
They started running toward the rowboat.
He dragged Jack and Annie down the beach as he ran after his men.
They got to the rowboat and pushed it into the sea.
Pinky and Stinky jumped into the boat.
Cap’n Bones let go of Jack and Annie.
He hauled himself into the rowboat.
Then the three pirates disappeared into the spray of the waves.
Just then the storm broke over the island.
I have to get the medallion!”
He ran to the hole dug by the pirates.
Even in the dreary light, the medallion was shining.
Big, fat raindrops were falling into the hole, washing away the sand.
Jack saw a patch of wood.
Then the rain cleared away more sand.
And Jack saw the top of an old trunk.
Was it Captain Kidd’s treasure chest?
She was halfway up the tree house ladder.
Jack kept staring at the chest.
Now Annie was shouting from the tree house window.
But Jack couldn’t tear himself away.
He brushed the rest of the muddy sand off the chest.
She was perched on the black rock.
He stared into her wise eyes.
He thought he knew her —knew her from somewhere else.
It was definitely time to go.
Jack took one last look at the treasure chest.
Then he took off, running toward the tree house.
His socks and rain boots were still there.
He quickly pulled the boots on.
He shoved the socks into his backpack.
The rope ladder was dancing wildly in the wind.
The ladder swayed as Jack climbed.
He was tossed this way and that.
At last he pulled himself into the tree house.
Annie was already holding the Pennsylvania book.
She pointed to the picture of Frog Creek.
The wind was already blowing hard.
But now it blew even harder.
The tree house started to spin.
Rain was dripping from the leaves of the tree.
They were back in Frog Creek.
He was still holding the gold medallion.
“I was hoping she might come back with us.”
“No magic creature has ever come back with us,” said Jack.
It was damp with rain and saltwater.
Jack took out the pirate book.
He put it on the stack of books.
On top of the dinosaur book.
Then Jack put the gold medallion beside the bookmark with the letter M.
Next he went down onto his knees.
And ran his finger over the shimmering M on the floor.
“We didn’t find any M’s on this trip,” he said.
The parrot swooshed into the tree house.
She perched on the stack of books.
Slowly Polly raised her bright green wings.
They grew bigger and bigger until they spread out like a huge green cape.
Then, in a great swirl of colors—in a blur of feathers and light—in a flapping and stretching and screeching—a new being took shape.
Polly was not a parrot any longer.
In her place was an old woman.
A beautiful old woman with long white hair and piercing eyes.
She wore a green feathered cape.
She perched on the stack of books.
And she was very calm and very still.
Neither Jack nor Annie could speak.
Hello, Annie,” the old woman said.
I’m the M person,” said Morgan.
“Have you ever heard of King Arthur?”
“Well, I am King Arthur’s sister,” said Morgan.
“What did you read about me, Jack?”
“You can’t believe everything you read, Jack.”
But I’m also a librarian,” said Morgan.
And I’ve come to the 20th century, your time, to collect books.
You are lucky to be born in a time with so many books.”
“I travel in this tree house to collect words from many different places around the world.
And from many different time periods.”
I want to borrow them for our scribes to copy.”
“Did you put all the bookmarks in them?”
You see, I like the pictures in the books.
Sometimes I want to visit the scenes in the pictures.
So all the bookmarks mark places I wish to go.”
“I placed a spell on the tree house,” said Morgan.
“So when I point to a picture and make the wish, the tree house takes me there.”
“I think you dropped this in dinosaur times,” said Jack.
He handed the gold medallion to Morgan.
I wondered where I’d lost it,” she said.
She put the medallion into a hidden pocket in her cape.
“You two are the only ones besides me to do it.
No one else has ever even seen my tree house before.”
“I had no idea it would ever be discovered.
But then you two came along.
Somehow you hooked right into my magic.”
“Well, for two reasons, I think,” explained Morgan.
So she actually saw the tree house.
And her belief helped you to see it, Jack.”
“Then you picked up a book, Jack.
And because you love books so much, you caused my magic spell to work.”
“You can’t imagine my dismay when you started to take off for dinosaur times.
I had to make a very quick decision.
And I decided to come along.”
“And the cat and the knight and Polly!”
“You were all these things to help us?”
“Yes, but I must go home now.
The people in Camelot need my help.”
She picked up Jack’s backpack and handed it to him.
Jack and Annie picked up their raincoats.
asked Annie, as they put their raincoats on.
She smiled at both of them.
“You remind me too much of myself.
Morgan le Fay touched Annie’s forehead gently.
Annie left the tree house first.
They climbed down the rope ladder for the last time.
They stood below the oak tree and looked up.
Morgan was looking out the window.
Her long white hair blew in the breeze.
Suddenly the wind began to blow.
A loud whistling sound filled the air.
Jack covered his ears and squeezed his eyes shut.
Annie and Jack stood a moment, staring up at the empty oak tree.
He felt too sad to speak.
As they started walking, he put his hands into his pockets.
Jack pulled out the gold medallion.
“Morgan must have put it there,” she said.
“I think it means she’ll be coming back.”
He clutched the medallion as he and Annie took off through the wet, sunny woods.
As they walked, the sun shined through the woods.
And all the wet leaves sparkled.
Leaves, branches, puddles, bushes, grass, vines, wild flowers—all glittered like jewels.
Annie had been right, thought Jack.
